CausalChain: MCM5 upregulation -> Synergistic interaction with RAD51 (in the context of an altered MCM5/MCM7 balance and KMT5C modulation) -> Aberrant activation of DSBR via error-prone break-induced replication -> Increased genomic instability -> Enhanced metastatic potential and poor prognosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, an upregulation of MCM5—relative to MCM7—establishes a unique, synergistic partnership with RAD51 that directs DSBR through an error-prone break-induced replication mechanism. This mechanism is further fine-tuned by the epigenetic regulator KMT5C, which facilitates RAD51 complex formation, and by RAD54B, which integrates signals from the wnt/β-catenin pathway. Collectively, these interactions promote genomic instability and drive metastasis, resulting in poorer clinical outcomes. Our research will employ contemporary CRISPR screening approaches, single-cell analyses, and live-cell imaging to precisely delineate these interplays and explore their potential as therapeutic targets.
Abstract: In liver neoplasms, we propose that an altered balance between MCM5 and MCM7 expression—characterized by the upregulation of MCM5—drives a distinctive, error-prone activation of the DNA double‐strand break repair (DSBR) pathway via break-induced replication (BIR). Specifically, elevated levels of MCM5 promote a unique interaction with RAD51, which, when modulated by the epigenetic regulator KMT5C and further influenced by oncogenic signals via RAD54B and the wnt/β-catenin pathway, shifts DSBR towards error-prone repair. This cascade results in increased genomic instability, thereby enhancing metastatic potential and leading to poor clinical outcomes. To dissect these mechanisms and validate the model, we will leverage state-of-the-art CRISPR screening, single-cell transcriptomics, and live-cell imaging techniques.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis centered on a novel role for MCM5 in engaging RAD51 to drive aberrant DSBR through break-induced replication, leading to genomic instability and metastatic progression. The revised hypothesis builds directly on this causal chain while addressing key gaps: it clarifies the importance of distinguishing MCM5 from MCM7 by incorporating a dysregulated MCM5/MCM7 balance; it explicitly incorporates the role of the epigenetic regulator KMT5C to modulate RAD51 complex formation; and it extends the model by integrating the influence of RAD54B and wnt/β-catenin oncogenic signaling. Furthermore, the revised version enhances practical implementability by explicitly referencing advanced methodologies (CRISPR screening, single-cell analyses, live-cell imaging) to validate each step of the causal chain.
